Destroyer
dee-STROY-er
n.
From destroy, Latin destruere, to unbuild, from de (down) and struere (to build). Webster 1828: one who destroys or lays waste. In Exodus the word names the agent of the tenth plague, and in 1 Corinthians the agent that struck the murmurers.

Biblical Definition

The destroyer in Scripture is an agent under God’s command, not a rival power, and the Passover text is careful about this. For the LORD will pass through to smite the Egyptians; and when he seeth the blood upon the lintel, and on the two side posts, the LORD will pass over the door, and will not suffer the destroyer to come in unto your houses to smite you (Exodus 12:23). Two things are said in one verse: the LORD Himself passes through to smite, and the LORD does not suffer the destroyer to enter where the blood is. The destroyer acts only by permission, and the permission is withheld at every marked door. Paul names the same figure in his catalogue of wilderness judgments: Neither murmur ye, as some of them also murmured, and were destroyed of the destroyer (1 Corinthians 10:10) — murmuring, the sin that seems smallest in the list, is the one with the destroyer attached. Proverbs uses the word for a human character, and the association is bracing: Whoso robbeth his father or his mother, and saith, It is no transgression; the same is the companion of a destroyer (Proverbs 28:24). The man who steals from his parents and calls it nothing keeps company he has not chosen.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines DESTROYER as one who destroys, ruins, kills, or lays waste; a person or agent that demolishes, subverts, or brings to nothing.

expand to see more

DESTROYER, n. — One who destroys, ruins, or lays waste; one who kills or puts an end to.

An agent employed in destruction, whether human, angelic, or providential.

One who subverts or brings to nothing; as, the destroyer of a family, a fortune, or a reputation.

In Scripture, the angel employed in the tenth plague and in the judgment of the murmurers.

From Latin destruo, to unbuild, from de and struo, to build — the root also of structure and construct.

Key Scripture

Exodus 12:23 — "For the LORD will pass through to smite the Egyptians; and when he seeth the blood upon the lintel, and on the two side posts, the LORD will pass over the door, and will not suffer the destroyer to come in unto your houses to smite you."

1 Corinthians 10:10 — "Neither murmur ye, as some of them also murmured, and were destroyed of the destroyer."

Proverbs 28:24 — "Whoso robbeth his father or his mother, and saith, It is no transgression; the same is the companion of a destroyer."

Proverbs 12:7 — "The wicked are overthrown, and are not: but the house of the righteous shall stand."

Modern Corruption

Dualism — ancient Manichaean, medieval Cathar, and its modern popular form in which Satan is treated as God’s near-equal opponent — makes the destroyer an independent power, when Exodus 12:23 shows him permitted or forbidden entry at God’s word.

expand to see more

The grammar of Exodus 12:23 will not support two comparable powers. The LORD passes through to smite; the LORD sees the blood; the LORD passes over; and the LORD will not suffer the destroyer to come in. Every verb belongs to God, including the one that governs the destroyer. The same structure appears in Job, where Satan must ask permission twice and is given a boundary each time, and in Luke 22:31, where Satan desires to have the disciples and Christ has already prayed. A popular Christianity that pictures the Christian life as a contest between two roughly matched combatants, with the outcome hanging on the believer’s spiritual technique, has misread the whole doctrine of providence. The devil is a creature on a leash held by the God he hates.

1 Corinthians 10:10 supplies the sting the passage was written to deliver. Of all the wilderness sins Paul lists — idolatry, fornication, tempting Christ — the one he attaches the destroyer to is murmuring. Grumbling feels like the most private and least consequential of sins, a matter of tone rather than substance, and Scripture treats it as a verdict rendered against God’s government. Numbers 14 has the whole generation refused entry for it. The dictionary names this not as a curiosity but as the ordinary besetting sin of comfortable believers, and Philippians 2:14 gives the plain command: Do all things without murmurings and disputings.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew mashchith (H4889), a destroyer, a ruin; shachath (H7843), to spoil, to ruin; Greek olothreutes (G3644), the destroyer; Apollyon (G623), the destroyer, in Revelation 9:11.

expand to see more

Hebrew mashchith (H4889) — a destroyer, that which ruins; the destroyer of Exodus 12:23.

Hebrew shachath (H7843) — to corrupt, to spoil, to destroy; the root behind mashchith.

Greek olothreutes (G3644) — the destroyer; used only at 1 Corinthians 10:10.

Greek Apolluon (G623) — Apollyon, the destroyer; the Greek name of the angel of the bottomless pit, called Abaddon in Hebrew (Revelation 9:11).

Greek gogguzo (G1111) — to murmur, to mutter; the sin to which the destroyer was attached.

Usage

"Will not suffer the destroyer to come in unto your houses (Exodus 12:23) — an agent permitted or forbidden at God’s word."

"Were destroyed of the destroyer (1 Corinthians 10:10) — and the sin named is murmuring."

"The same is the companion of a destroyer (Proverbs 28:24) — company a man keeps without choosing it."
